Project scope
What is a project scope? Take dadmor’s real template, free
Most fights in website projects are not about code at all. They are about one sentence nobody ever wrote down. This article is the cure for those sentences, and yes, it is free.
21 November 2026·8 min read·Roxana and Arshia

In this article

  1. What a project scope is, and what it is not
  2. Our scope template, section by section
  3. Three classic fights this one sheet of paper switches off
  4. Tonight, in half an hour, write your own
  5. Write it down

Summary

  1. A scope is a project’s shared memory. Anything that is not written down looks different inside each person’s head.
  2. The most important section is not the feature list. It is the list of what is NOT in the project.
  3. One page that gets read and signed beats ten pages of contract that nobody opens.

This is our scope template, in full. The same document we put on the table and sign before any project starts. Take it to a competitor and you will still get a better project, and the whole market gets a bit healthier for it. A good scope does not make the client ours. It saves the project. That is exactly why we do not hide it.

You can fill it in for your own project tonight. Under every section there is a filled example from a made up shop, and under that, the exact fight that line prevents when it exists, and starts when it does not.
What a project scope is, and what it is not

A project scope is a short document. It says what will be built, who for, with what content, in what time, and by what measure it counts as done. It is not a legal contract and it does not replace a lawyer. It is not a quote either: the quote is simply the price of this document. The scope is the picture both sides hold in common, before money and time get spent.

Skip it, and each side builds the project in their own head. In yours there is a complete shop, every detail in place. In the builder’s head there is a simple brochure site. You are both telling the truth, that is the miserable part. Then delivery day arrives, two different products are sitting on the table, and the fight starts right there. A scope is just those two pictures made into one, on paper, on day one.
Our scope template, section by section
Our template has ten sections. No fewer, because every single one was born out of a real fight. No more, because a document nobody reads prevents no fights at all. Here it is:

The dadmor scope template, as we actually use it

Ready to copy

1Project goal

The project’s goal, in one sentence. A sentence every later decision can be measured against.

Example: Selling the shop’s products online, on the website, instead of taking every order by hand in DMs.

The fight it prevents: if the goal will not fit in one sentence, every shiny new feature looks essential halfway through, and nobody can say no.

2Audience and customer

Who the main customer is, where they come from, and what device they show up on.

Example: The page’s existing customers, plus people searching on Google. Most of them arrive on a phone.

The fight it prevents: without it, the design quietly gets built for the builder’s taste, not for your actual customer.

3Pages

The full list of pages, by name. If a page is not on this list, it is not in this project.

Example: Home, shop, product page, basket and checkout, about, contact, buying and returns policy.

The fight it prevents: an unlisted page gets requested on the last day, as a small favour, and it blows up the whole schedule.

4Features

Every feature written as one complete sentence you could test. Never an adjective.

Example: Payment through a bank gateway, percentage discount codes, tracking an order by its number, an SMS when the order status changes.

The fight it prevents: words like “a complete shop” or “a professional panel” mean something different to everyone in the room. A full sentence makes the meaning one thing.

5Content

Who prepares the words and photos for each page, and the date they hand them over.

Example: Words for every page come from the client by the end of week two. The client takes the product photos; colour correction and cropping sit with the builder.

The fight it prevents: most launch delays are not code. They are content that was meant to arrive and did not, with no name and no date written anywhere.

6Connections

Every outside system the site has to talk to, named one by one.

Example: The bank payment gateway, the SMS panel, work email on the domain.

The fight it prevents: every connection drags in a third party, a separate cost and a separate test. One nobody wrote down surfaces mid project, and costs more there.

7Out of scope

The things that are explicitly not part of this project. However obvious they feel.

Example: Producing Instagram content, advertising, entering 500 old products, designing a logo.

The fight it prevents: the most important section in the whole template. Most fights are work one side assumed was in, and the other assumed was out.

8Schedule and delivery points

The date of each stage, and exactly what gets handed over that day.

Example: End of week three: a version of the shop you can click through. End of week five: live, on the main domain.

The fight it prevents: one final date with nothing in the middle means nobody knows if the work is ahead or behind until the last day, when nothing can be done about it.

9Acceptance criteria

What “finished” actually means, and the test that proves it.

Example: A complete purchase, made with a real card, with an invoice issued. The site reads and works properly on phones, and on Chrome and Firefox.

The fight it prevents: without criteria, delivery becomes two tired people’s taste on one tiring day. That fight has no winner.

10Changes after signing

How a new request, mid project, gets its price and its effect on the schedule, and where it lands in the queue.

Example: Anything outside this document is quoted in writing first, price and schedule effect included, and only gets built once the client approves it.

The fight it prevents: change itself is natural, projects breathe. Unruled change is what kills them. This line makes change possible, and safe.
For most website projects, ten sections is enough. If yours is bigger, add detail inside the sections. Just do not delete one. Especially not section seven.
A scope is not paperwork for its own sake. It is the project’s shared memory, and human memory, unlike paper, remembers it differently every day.
Three classic fights this one sheet of paper switches off

“Just add one page.” Said mid project, it sounds harmless. But a page means design, build, content and testing. With a signed page list, that sentence gets a clean answer: yes, at this price, and it moves the schedule by this much. No fight, no one sided favour.

“I thought payment was included.” The most common sentence on delivery day. One side swears it was discussed, the other swears it was not, and both memories are honest. Only a features section and an out of scope section, written down, can answer that sentence before anyone has to say it.

“It was supposed to be ready before the holiday.” One final date and no stops along the way means no warning, anywhere. Give week three a named delivery and falling behind shows up in week three, while something can still be done. Not the night before the holiday.
Tonight, in half an hour, write your own
You do not have to wait for anyone to do this. Get a sheet of paper and go in this order:

items: Write the goal in one sentence. If the sentence needs two “ands”, you have not found the goal yet.
List the pages. Stuck? Open the site of a competitor you like and count theirs.
Write features as full sentences, not adjectives. “Payment through a gateway” is a sentence. “A professional shop” is just an adjective.
Do not leave out of scope empty. Write down the three things you are sure are obviously not included. Especially those three.
Give the content a name and a date: who hands over what, by when.

blocks.html: Now take that sheet to any builder you like. For the first time, every quote you get is priced against the same scope, so they can actually be compared. Want our eyes on yours as well? Start at the website building page. A ready scope cuts the whole conversation in half.
Write it down

A scope is not there to make a project dry and bureaucratic. It has one job: turning what is in two different heads into one single thing, on paper, before the money and the time go out the door. Projects that end in fights almost never had a technical problem. They had a sentence that was never written. So write the sentence.
Scope in hand? Now see its number

With a scope written, the project estimator gives you a rough range in minutes. And the website building page shows how we work with this exact document: scope first, then a written proposal, then we build.
Frequently asked questions

What is a project scope?

It is a short document that says what gets built, who it is for, what content goes in it, how long it takes, and how everyone will know it is finished. It is not a legal contract, and it is not a quote. It is the picture both sides agree on before money and time start moving.

What is the most important part of a scope?

Not the feature list, surprisingly. It is the out of scope section, the things written down as not part of this project. Most fights are about work one side assumed was in, while the other side assumed it was out.

How many sections does the dadmor template have?

Ten: the project goal, the audience and customer, pages, features, content, connections, out of scope, schedule and delivery points, acceptance criteria, and changes after signing. For most website projects, those ten carry the whole thing.

What happens without a scope?

Each side builds the project inside their own head, and on delivery day there are two different products on the table. The fights are always the same: “Just add one page.” “I thought payment was included.” “It was supposed to be ready before the holiday.”
